full_judgment:
4. Mr. Mostafa Niaz Muhamucl, the learned Advocate for the appellant has taken me through the judgments of the Courts below. The learned Advocate submits that the judgment of the lower appellate Court is not a proper judgment of reversal in as much as he has reversed the finding of the learned Munsif without cogent reasons. Mr. A.K.M. Shafiqur Rahinan, the learned Advocate for the respondent supports the judgment of the lower appellate Court. 5. It appears from the judgment of the trial Court that the learned Munsif relying on the deed of agreement Ext. 4 itself and relying on the evidence of the plaintiff No. 1 (P.W. 2) and the evidence of P.W. 3 Ahmed Meah and P.W. 4 Barada Charan Baidya became satisfied about the plaintiff's alleged agreement of reconveyance. The learned Munsif has observed that P.Ws. 3 and 4 were the most competent witnesses in the case. The learned Munsif for being satisfied about the genuineness of the disputed document Ext. 4 also relied on the opinion of the handwriting expert (P.W. 1) who had opined that the defendant had executed Ext. 4 by signing his name. The learned trial court also compared the disputed signature of defendant on. the document Ext. 4 with his admitted signatures and became conviced that the defendant executed the document Ext. 4 by signing his name. The learned Subordinate Judge, in appeal, held that the opinion of the handwriting expert was not corroborated and could not be taken as final. The learned Subordinate Judge relied on certain variations between the disputed signature and specific signatures noticed by the handwriting expert and mentioned in his report. The expert also noticed variations in the word "2" in the specimen sig-natures with disputed signature. The learned Subordinate Judge has however failed to consider that the handwriting expert has considered the variations and has, Spite, been of the opinion that the signature of the defendant in Ext. 4 is I genuine signature. The opinion of the handwriting in expert to this effect after consideration of the variations was certainly mere worthy of credit than one if any he would have given without considering the variations. I am of the opinion that the learned Subordinate Judge has discarded the evidence of the band writing ex-pert and his opinion without cogent and sufficient reason. It also appears that the learned Subordinate Judge was looking for corroboration for the opinion of the expert. It could not be understood what corroborative evidence he was looking for. The opinion of the expert was itself opinion evidence and not a direct evidence of the disputed signature. No corroborative evidence could be necessary. The evidence, however, was not final. It appears that the learned trial Court itself compared the disputed signature with the admitted signatures and was convinced that the signature of the defendant in Ext. 4 was a genuine signature of the defendant. The learned Subordinate Judge does not appear even to have referred to this opinion arrived at by the learned trial Court after comparison of the disputed signature of the defendant with his admitted signatures which he was entitled to do under section 73 of the Evidence Act. Non-consideration of the opinion arrived at by the learned trial Court after comparison is a serious error of law. The learned Subordinate Judge has not also Himself compared the disputed signature with the admitted signatures and has not attempted to-form his own opinion about its genuineness. The learned Subordinate Judge appears to have relied on the evidence of the D.W.2 Abdul Malek and D.W.4 Abdur Rahman in coming to the conclusion that there was no agreement for sale. He has observed that D.Ws. 2 and 4 have stated that they were present at the time of execution of the kabala and at that time no agreement was executed. It, however, appears that these two witnesses did not claim to be present at the time of the execution or the kabala. It is therefore a clear misreading of the evidence of D.Ws.2 and 4. It also appears that the learned Subordinate. Judge has also referred to the evidence of D.W.3 Abdul Gani who stated that he was present at the time of the execution of the kabala. He stated that no agreement was executed at that time it appears from the evidence of defendant himself (D.W.1) that he did not say that D.W.3 was present at the time of execution of the kabala. According to him only the parties, the scribe and the attesting witnesses were present. The learned Subordinate Judge in failing to con-sider this case of the defendant made out in his evidence has erred in law and his judgment suffers from the defect of non-reading of evidence on a very material point. The learned trial Court has observed that D.Ws. 2; 3 and 4 were chance witnesses and this observation is not without foundation. Admittedly none of them were attesting witnesses of the kabala. The learned trial Court could not rely on their evidence. According to the plaintiff's case the deed of sale, which is an undisputed document and the deed of agreement were written at the same baithak. The scribe and attesting witnesses of both the documents are the same. The plaintiff examined himself, the scribe and an attesting witness. The otter attesting witness was deed. The plaintiff also obtained opinion of Handwriting expert and the opinion supported his case. Relying on these evidences which were evidently the best evidences and also comparing the disputed signature himself came to the conclusion that the defendant had agreed to reconvey the suit-land and executed the deed of agreement Ext.4, which proved the alleged agreement. The learned lower Appellate Court has reversed the finding of the learned trial Court without cogent reasons. His judgment cannot be said to be a proper judgment of reversal. The learned trial Court has seen the witnesses and has observed that the credibility of P.Ws. 2, 3 and 4 were not shaken and relied on them. The learned lower appellate Court sitting in appeal not having had the opportunity of seeing the witnesses should have thought twice and more than twice before reversing the finding of the learned trial Court. In the case of Radha Prasad Singh Vs. Gajadhar Singh and ors. AIR 1960 S.C. 115 decided by the Indian Supreme Court, it was observed that "all the courts in all the cases have stressed the rule which the courts of appeal should observe for themselves: that a judge sitting on appeal not having had the opportunity of seeing and hearing the witnesses should think twice and more than twice before reversing the finding of fact arrived at by the trial Court who had that opportunity." In the case of Sarju Perhad Vs. Avaleshawar. Pratap Narain Singh, A.I.R. 1951 (SC) 120, the Supreme Court of India laid down the rule: "The rule is-and it is nothing more than a rule of practice—that where there is conflict of oral evidence of the parties on any matter in issue and the decision hinges upon the credibility of the witnesses, then unless there is some special feature about the evidence of a particular witness which has escaped the trial Judge's notice or there is sufficient balance of improbability to displace his opinion as to where the credibility lies, the appellate Court should not interfere with the finding of trial Court on a question of fact." 

 6. In the case of Badruddin Khan Vs. Bangladesh and another reported in (1984) 34 DLR (AD) 52, the Appellate Division has quoted with approval the observations of the Indian Supreme Court in the two decision referred to above in reversing a decision of the High Court Division. In the case before me, I have already observed that there has been a misreading of evidence by the appellate Court and also a non-consideration of the opinion of the trial Court on the genuineness of the disputed document which was also good evidence on the point. The judgment of reversal of the lower appellate Court is not a proper judgment of reversal and can-not be sustained.
